title: Bounce-Back Candidates
brief: Which players had a down season from injury, role or a shooting or steals slump and could return to their earlier level? It must explain why one bad season should not set the price and which bounce-backs depend on unstable stats.
summary: One bad season should not set a player's price. Injuries, role changes and shooting or steals slumps often reverse, and drafters fear last year's injuries more than they should. In our auction, pay for bounce-backs that rest on health, role and real skills such as FT% and a long steals record. Keep bids small or wait on waivers when the case needs an unstable stat like a FG% jump or a career-high steal rate to return.

sections.heading: Why one bad season should not set the price

paragraphs.text: One bad season does not make a player bad. Do not price anyone on a single year. Look at his longer record and ask why the last season went wrong. If the cause was an injury, a role change or a slump that is now gone, his earlier level is the better guide.

Do not let one season flip a long-term story either. A player who was reliable for years and then missed time is not suddenly injury prone. A player who was injury prone for years is not safe after one healthy season. Set your value from the long record before the auction on 2026-10-18 and stick to it in the room.

Drafters worry too much about players coming back from an injury that ruined last season. You can trust them more than their ADP suggests. In our auction, that means you can keep bidding on these players up to your own pre-set value even when the room goes quiet. A cheap market price is often the injury fear, not the player.

Bounce-back candidates come from three places: role changes, injuries and shooting slumps. Sort every candidate into one of these groups before the draft. Each group has a different early check. Role cases need minutes and usage. Injury cases need health reports and minutes. Slump cases need the percentages themselves.

A lower shooting percentage can recover when a player's usage drops. Fewer forced shots often means better ones. This matters in our league because FG% is a team ratio. A high-volume shooter who goes from poor to average efficiency helps your team FG% more than a low-volume player with a good percentage. When a player moves next to a stronger scorer or a better passer, treat his FG% as likely to improve, not as fixed at last year's number.

sections.heading: Which stats rebound and which are unstable

paragraphs.text: Several players had big free throw drops for no clear reason. Treat that as a pattern that will likely revert. A FT% drop with no injury or mechanics story is one of the safer bounce-backs to pay for. Bid on the career FT% rate, not last season's.

Steals swing in both directions from year to year. Never pay for a career-high steal rate, because it is the stat most likely to fall back. A player whose steals dropped is a different case. If he has a long record of high steals, he can bounce back. Separate those two cases before you bid on any steals specialist.

The least stable bounce-backs depend on FG% or three-point percentage coming back after an injury or a role change. They can happen, but only if health and usage go the right way. Pay a modest price for these players. Check their percentages in the first two to three weeks before you trust them in your lineup.

sections.heading: Where the experts differ on steals

paragraphs.text: The notes lean in different directions on steals. One note uses elastic band theory: steals are an elite skill, so a down year should snap back toward the player's normal level. Another note stresses that steals are variable in both directions and warns against paying for any one year's rate. Both agree a drop can reverse. They differ on how much you should trust that. A middle path for our league: pay a fair price for a player with several strong steals seasons and one down year, but do not add a premium for the expected rebound.

sections.heading: How to use this in our auction and on waivers

paragraphs.text: Early in the auction, only pay full price for bounce-backs that rest on health and role, where the skills were never in doubt. In the middle of the draft, target slump cases tied to FT% or a long steals record at prices near the current market. Do not go back to what our league paid last season. Late, near the 144-player cutoff, take FG% and shooting rebounds for 1 to 5 USD. Leave the weakest cases on waivers and watch them.

After the draft, track minutes, usage and the key percentage for each bounce-back in the first weeks. Waivers process daily with a limit of 6 adds per week. That leaves room to drop a late flyer whose role did not come back and add one whose FG% did. Keep some FAB for players left undrafted whose shooting recovers early.
